name: Reishi (Ganoderma lucidum, lingzhi)
short: Case reports: fatal fulminant hepatitis after reishi powder, other liver injury. Cochrane review, type 2 diabetes (one 84-person trial): adverse events non-serious, not significantly above placebo.
text: Case reports describe liver injury with reishi: a fatal case of fulminant hepatitis and an earlier case of hepatotoxicity, both in patients who had taken boiled lingzhi without problems but developed liver toxicity 1 to 2 months after switching to lingzhi powder, and who had also taken other therapeutic agents (the authors called for close monitoring, especially in combination with other drugs); acute hepatitis in a 47-year-old man after reishi mushroom powder (the report names the species Ganoderma lingzhi) taken with alcohol, which resolved within two weeks; and marked eosinophilia with liver nodules and slightly raised liver enzymes in a 61-year-old man, which resolved after he stopped the product. A Cochrane review of 5 trials (398 participants) used data from three placebo-controlled trials, all in people with type 2 diabetes taking reishi for 12 to 16 weeks; the abstract says that, apart from the analyses of HbA1c, total cholesterol, LDL cholesterol and body-mass index (from two studies), all analyses came from a single study of 84 participants, and it reports that participants who took reishi for four months were 1.67 times as likely as those on placebo to have an adverse event, a difference that was not statistically significant (95% CI 0.86 to 3.24), and these were not serious side effects. In a cross-sectional survey of 1,374 Chinese cancer patients using reishi products, 9.1% reported adverse events, including dry mouth, constipation, insomnia, itching and vertigo. An analysis of the WHO VigiBase reporting database of adaptogenic and immune-modulating natural products found that, among reports naming a single-ingredient product as the sole suspect, 15.8% were serious, including eight fatal cases (the abstract does not say which products these involved), and that reishi was among the products most frequently associated with serious adverse events, although causality was unclear. In a small study, reishi taken by mouth for 2 weeks inhibited platelet aggregation in patients with atherosclerotic disease; the abstract does not report bleeding or name any interacting medicine.
